> ## Regarding dealing with possible infeasible cases.

Again, as demonstrated by our experiments, editing a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs in a single LP using our method is feasible for real-world applications in practice. However, we agree that there could be infeasible cases for a specific combination of a pre-trained DNN, a edit set and gradient constraints. Here we provide possible directions to handle such infeasible cases based on our method, and leave it as future work.

1. One can edit the DNN from a different layer.
2. One can constrain each input of the edit set on a linear piece other than the original linear piece. In the activation condition constraint (Eq. 10), ProGrad uses the original linear piece, expressed by $\textrm{diag}(1_{\textrm{z}^{(\ell)}>0})$, as the the default choice of linear piece to constrain one input to lie on. However, one can use a different heuristics to choose a different linear piece, e.g., flip one element in $\textrm{diag}(1_{\textrm{z}^{(\ell)}>0})$.
3. One can iteratively call ProGrad to edit the weights of multiple layers in "multiple steps" **in an accumulative manner**. For example, given an $L$ layer ReLU DNN $\mathcal{N}$ and an edit set $\chi$, one can split $\chi$ into subsets $\chi_1$, $\chi_2$ and $\chi_3$, firstly edit layers $\mathcal{N}[\ell_1:L]$ to edit the subset $\chi_1$; then **accumulatively** edit layers $\mathcal{N}[\ell_2:L]$ to edit the subset $\chi_1 \cup \chi_2$, where constraints for $\chi_1$ is already satisfied and we use ProGrad to preserve the constraint-satisfaction when editing layers $\mathcal{N}[\ell_2:L]$; finally edit layers $\mathcal{N}[\ell_3:L]$ to **accumulatively** edit the entire edit set $\chi \coloneqq \chi_1 \cup \chi_2 \cup \chi_3$ to get a DNN that satisfies the constraints for all inputs in $\chi$.

> ## Regarding the difference from APRNN.

APRNN and ProGrad share the same idea of using activation condition constraints to constrain each input in the edit set to lie on a specific linear piece of the edited DNN. **Note that the linear piece is not fixed but variable**, because it is expressed as a closed-form linear expression in terms of the editable DNN parameters. In particular, the APRNN activation condition constraint (Eq. 10) is the same as ours (Eq. 18).

**The difference**: APRNN focuses on the **forward pass** of a DNN, hence provides and proves the construction of the **variable outputs** in terms of the editable DNN parameters (Eq. 7–9); this work focuses on the **backward pass** of a DNN, hence provides and proves the construction of the **variable input gradients** in terms of the editable DNN parameters (Eq. 16–17, 19–20).

Thank you for your response and for giving us a chance to clarify the ideas in the paper.

> ## Regarding editing a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs.

We would like to stress that, for each setting of our experiments, **ProGrad does edit a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs on real-world DNNs and gradient constraints** by calling the LP solver **once** to **solve a single LP** (the construction of this single LP is presented and proved in Appendix B). In particular:
- Section 5.1 (Table 1 and Line 213-214): The GradCAM editing on ImageNet ResNet152 DNN experiment consists of two settings: in the first setting, ProGrad edits a set of **100 inputs** in one LP within 4 hours; in the second setting, ProGrad edits a set of **1,000 inputs** in one LP within 4 hours.
- Section 5.2 (Table 2 and Line 233-235): The IG editing on SST2 Llama LLM experiment consists of two settings: in the first setting, ProGrad edits a set of **100 inputs** in one LP within 10 minutes; in the second setting, ProGrad edits a set of **200 inputs** in one LP within 10 minutes.
- Section 5.3 (Line 672 in Appendix C.3): ProGrad edits a set of **2,048 inputs** in one LP within 10 seconds.

As evidenced by our experimental results, editing a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs in a single LP using our method is feasible. **A similar empirical observation has been made in prior work such as APRNN and PREPARED**, which also solve a single LP problem that constrains hundreds of inputs.

> ## Intuition for "why should one expect the problem to be feasible".

Regarding the problem of editing a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs in a single LP,
here we provide an intuition for why should one expect it to be feasible **in our post-training use case**. Note that **for each linear piece** of a DNN, **the variable input gradient is a different closed-form linear expression** in terms of the editable DNN parameters. Real-world pre-trained DNNs are over-parameterized, and the number of linear pieces grows exponentially as the width and depth of the DNN. Hence, the hundreds to thousands of (meaningful real-world) inputs in the edit set are **very likely to lie on different linear pieces**, effectively reducing the chance of getting a conflict.

The above intuition is corroborated by our experimental results where the single LP for editing a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs is feasible.
A similar empirical observation has been made in prior work such as APRNN and PREPARED, which also solve a single LP problem that constrains hundreds of inputs.

Furthermore, we would like to clarify that training a new DNN from scratch is **not** the use case proposed in this paper. We agree that one should not expect to train a new DNN from scratch on all of the training data by solving a single LP.

> ## Regarding the usage of ProGrad.

In this paper, we proposed to use ProGrad as a **post-training** method, that is editing a pre-trained DNN on a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs, which is practical as demonstrated in our experiments, and useful in practice to correct the gradient behavior on those inputs, in the context of repairing a pre-trained DNN. Note that ProGrad is the only method that is able to enforce hard gradient constraints on a set of hundreds to thousands of inputs.

Furthermore, beyond the hundreds to thousands of inputs in the edit set, **our method does help reduce similar mistakes**: the gradient edit to the edit set does generalize to similar inputs that are not in the edit set, and such generalization on ProGrad-edited DNNs also outperformed the baselines.

For example, for the Grad-CAM experiment on ResNet152 with 1000 inputs (Section 5.1), here we present the Grad-CAM metrics, namely constraint satisfaction rate (Constr. Sat.) with $\varepsilon$=1e-1, cosine similarity (Cos.) and intersection over union (IoU), **on a set of similar inputs that is similar to but disjoint from the edit set** (same corruption type but different severity level). **As evidenced by the results, our method (ProGrad) improves those Grad-CAM metrics comparing to the original model, and achieves the best results comparing to the fine-tuning baselines.**

| Method   |   Constr. Sat. |       Cos. |        IoU |
|:---------|---------------:|-----------:|-----------:|
| Original |         32.98% |     77.53% |     39.42% |
| EWA      |         35.71% |     82.41% |     39.89% |
| SWA      |         36.15% |     84.74% |     45.28% |
| SSWA     |         36.16% |     84.74% |     45.26% |
| **ProGrad**  |     **42.35%** | **85.75%** | **47.43%** |

We would like to clarify that the LP size is (qualitatively) analyzed in the proof in Appendix A. In the revision, we will further clarify it and provide a detailed definition of the LP size as a function of the network depth/width.

> ## Regarding example gradient constraints in real-world control systems and scientific applications (Question 4 and Weakness 1, 3).

For control systems, enforcing monotonicity for glucose-insulin dynamics [c1], bounding gradients to reduce action oscillations [c2] are examples of safety constraints that can be expressed in terms of gradients. For scientific applications such as density functional theory (DFT), the neural network approximating the density functional must satisfy hard gradient constraints [c3].

In this work we focus on enforcing hard Grad-CAM and IG constraints for real-world vision and natural language applications, demonstrating the real-world applicability of gradient editing in the context of explainable AI. We leave further investigation on control systems and scientific computation applications as our future work.

[c1] Kushner, Taisa, Sriram Sankaranarayanan, and Marc Breton. "Conformance verification for neural network models of glucose-insulin dynamics." Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Hybrid Systems: Computation and Control. 2020.

[c2] Majd, Keyvan, et al. "Safe Robot Learning in Assistive Devices through Neural Network Repair." Conference on Robot Learning. PMLR, 2023.

[c3] Pokharel, Kanun, et al. "Exact constraints and appropriate norms in machine-learned exchange-correlation functionals." The Journal of Chemical Physics 157.17 (2022).

> ## Regarding "learning with less data" (Question 4 and Weakness 1).

We would like to clarify that we did not mean to imply that our technique can be used to train a DNN from scratch with less data. By "learning with less data" we mean "learning constraints with less data", that is, explicitly incorporating the constraints into the network, instead of relying on the network to "infer" these constraints implicitly from the data alone. In the revision we will clarify this.

The experiment in Figure 1 demonstrates how ProGrad can be used to get a network that satisfies hard gradient constraints that is not guaranteed by training with data alone. This is also evidenced by our experiments on real-world ResNet152 DNN and Llama LLM, where our technique is the only technique that can enforce hard complex Grad-CAM/IG constraints.

Such augmentation of data with constraints serves as a general motivation for constraint-based learning. Our primary contribution is a novel technique to enforce hard gradient constraints in DNNs, which we have evaluated on real-world data and networks in computer vision and natural language processing. Investigating how this new primitive could be used to reduce the need for training data would be an interesting future direction.

> ## Regarding the layers we allow to edit.

As presented in the Appendix B in the supplementary material, we would like to clarify that our approach is able to edit the parameters of **any layer** and the biases of the subsequent layers for a piecewise-linear DNN. Our approach is not restricted to only modifying the weight of the first layer. For ease of exposition, the main paper presents our approach for editing the first layer weights and other layer biases.

> ## Regarding the effectiveness of our approach on complex constraints.

Our experiments demonstrates that our approach is effective and practical for real-world DNNs. The Grad-CAM and IG constraints we used in our experiments are complex, and our results on real-world ResNet and LLM demonstrate that editing the last few layers is sufficient for the (often over-parameterized) real-world DNNs to satisfy these complex constraints.

> ## Regarding editing multiple layers' weights using Quadratic Programming (QP).

Yes our approach can naturally be extended to edit multiple layers' weights using Quadratic Programming (QP). In theory, this gives a larger solution space and could improve the feasibility. However, in practice, using QP could be significantly slower than LP, making the editing non-scalable. Consider the experiment in section 5.3 as an example, for a ReLU version of the 4-layer fully-connected DNN with 100 hidden neurons per layer, for the same constraints and objectives on 2048 input points:
  - editing the last layer using LP takes 10 seconds;
  - editing the second last layer's parameters and the last layer's bias using LP takes 1 minute;
  - editing the last two layers using QP *timeouts in 2 hours*.

Furthermore, as demonstrated in our experiments, using LP is sufficient to edit real-world models against complex gradient constraints like Grad-CAM and IG.

> ## Regarding the runtime for the experiments.

As included in the Appendix C, for the ResNet Grad-CAM experiment (Section 5.1), ProGrad finished in under 4 hours for each of the two settings; for the LLM IG experiment (Section 5.2), ProGrad finished in under 600 seconds for each of the two settings. The runtime of ProGrad demonstrates the scalability of our approach.

Specifically, in the LLM IG experiment, ProGrad took 501 seconds for the 100 samples setting and 562 seconds for the 200 samples setting. In the revision, we will include the specific runtime results.

> ## Regarding Lipschitz NN.

We believe this is an interesting and important direction and we leave it as our future work.

> ## Regarding the related verification work.

In the revision we will include and discuss those related verification work.

> ## Regarding the trade-off in editing more layers.

In terms of the feasibility, editing an earlier layers' parameters and the subsequent layers' biases does not necessarily improve feasibility comparing to editing a later layer's parameters and the the subsequent layers' biases. Because the set of editable parameters (the solution space) for editing from an earlier layer is not a super set of the set of the case of editing from a later layer. In practice, if the user is not satisfied with the result of editing from a later layer, the user could then try to edit from an earlier layer.

In terms of the efficiency, because editing from an earlier leads to more LP constraints compared to editing from a later layer, it is often expected to take a longer time.

> ## Regarding polytope editing.

As stated in the limitation, our approach is not addressing enforcing gradient constraints over input polytopes, and cannot be directly applied to enforce robustness, for instance.

However, we would like to stress that our experiments related to enforcing gradient-based attributions in computer vision and LLM-based natural language processing demonstrate the real-world applicability of pointwise gradient editing, in the context of explainable AI.

> ## Regarding the novelty and contribution.

To the best of our knowledge, our approach (ProGrad) is the first efficient approach for enforcing hard gradient constraints on DNNs that runs in polynomial time (Theorem 4.3).

Our key contribution is the novel *conditional variable gradient* of DNN, which generalizes the prior work (APRNN) to handle the gradient of DNN. We are the first to propose the construction of the conditional variable gradient for the backward pass of DNNs, and proved their soundness.

We also identified real-world applications of enforcing hard gradient constraints in the context of explainable AI (Grad-CAM and IG). We demonstrated the practicality and scalability of our approach on real-world DNNs in computer vision and natural language processing. We would like to stress that *our approach is the only approach that is able to enforce those complex gradient hard constraints*, significantly outperforms prior approaches.

summary.value: This work proposes provable gradient editing using linear programming by relaxing nonlinear constant exact gradient of the deep neural networks (with ReLU activations) to linear variable gradients under constraint activation condition. While input/output constraint prior methods are available ProGrad is novel in applying constraints on gradients. Linear gradient expression and the activation condition is polynomial in the size and scales well.The authors present three applications: enforcing GradCAM constraints on ResNet152, Integrated Gradients (IG) on a Llama 3 LLM, and physical gradient constraints in scientific computation tasks. Their evaluation setting contains perturbed input which results in misclassification in the baseline  that is fixed by ProGrad by applying the constraints and solving with Linear Programming. Empirical evidence supports the author's claims about performance.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1. The paper introduces the previously unaddressed problem of provable gradient editing i.e. editing DNN parameters to satisfy hard constraints on input gradients, rather than just output constraints. This is a significant and timely contribution.
2. Overall paper is clearly written with a well defined premise of definitions, theorems, proofs and overall mathematical rigor. Theorem 4.3 is the most fundamental one that is simple and elegant to follow and connects the relaxed problem to an LP, making what would otherwise be NP-hard tractable. This makes it to be solved by off the shelf LP solver in this case Gurobi.  
3. Performance achieved as measured by Constraint satisfaction, Cosine similarity, IOU, Classification Accuracy beats other fine tuning based methods. In all the cases it achieves 100% constraint satisfaction which is the main aim of the paper. So the main claim is well supported in results.
4. Wider domain coverage: Deep neural networks on image and language as well as control system proxy with simpler trigonometric function has been tested. 
5. Limitations are honestly acknowledged as the input is chosen to be constant unlike a polytope in most practical scenarios. Paper indicates some steps that can be taken from prior work to achieve this which is a good start.


Weaknesses:

1. Introduction lacks sufficient details about the motivation of adding constraints on gradients. It briefly explains grad cam attribution in fig.2, but lacks more details about other ways in which it can be used. For example it talks about requiring less data for training deep neural networks but does not sufficiently describe how or validate ProGrad indeed helps in this regard. 
2. Real-world LPs for large networks can still be computationally expensive. Therefore analysis of LP size and solve time as a function of network depth/width is required.
3. It only simulates the Control system application using a simpler trigonometric function. Effect on real scientific and safety critical control systems remains unexplored.
4. Lack of qualitative samples. Typically it is expected to provide more samples in supplementary but none other than a single sample in the main paper is provided. It would also help to showcase which samples are harder to be constrained and if there are any patterns.

summary.value: ProGrad provides a helpful way to enforce constraints on the gradients of neural networks by editing their parameters. The experimental evaluations show how ProGrad can be used in interpretability (enforcing grad-cam constraints), editing weights of neural networks to fix hallucinations (llama 3), and in sys id and controls. The work shows significant improvement over just finetuning the models.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths

* Strong constraint enforcement is a great strength and the theory appears comprehensive.

* The ability to maintain these constraints is impactful in a few domains (interpretability, editing, sys id)

* The results show significant improvement in constraint satisfaction over just finetuning the models

Weaknesses

* I am uncertain if strictly enforcing gradients is helpful for some of the proposed applications. Example: does enforcing the gradient constraints on misclassified samples for LLama help reduce similar mistakes on held-out samples? Or is finetuning better in this case?  

Another example: in the system identification example in Section 5.3, what if the gradient of the function is not well behaved (such as it shooting to infinity at 0 or something else like that)? Will the system actually be approximated/identified accurately?

* Missing reference and discussion of a highly relevant work on enforcing hard constraints in [1]

[1] Sridhar et al, Guaranteed Conformance of Neurosymbolic (World) Models to Natural Constraints, L4DC 2023

summary.value: The paper proposes to edit the gradient of deep neural networks to satisfy hard polytope constraints by solving linear programming. The method is rooted in the formal verification of neural networks and is well-suited for constraint satisfaction. The experiments show some examples of potential applications on vision, LLM and NN training.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

- This paper is interesting. The topic of gradient satisfaction is important but challenging. The examples of the paper show potential applications in vision and LLMs. I believe it is also promising in formal methods and dynamical systems.

summary.value: This paper introduces ProGrad , a method for editing the parameters of a deep neural network (DNN) to enforce hard constraints on its gradients. The key idea is to model DNN gradients using what the authors call a conditional variable gradient , which allows the originally non-linear and complex gradient constraint enforcement task to be reduced to solving a linear program (LP) . This makes it possible to efficiently find minimal parameter changes that ensure the DNN satisfies the desired gradient constraints.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
- Strengths:
  - This is an important and valuable research topic.
  - The paper is very well-written.
  - This work proposes an algorithm capable of provably enforcing hard gradient constraints on DNNs, not just soft regularization or empirical fine-tuning.
  - The conditional variable gradient formulation is mathematically well-grounded and allows for reducing the originally non-linear gradient editing problem into a linear programming one. This is a significant theoretical contribution.
  - The method is tested on diverse architectures and tasks — CNNs, LLMs, and regression functions, showing consistent success in satisfying gradient constraints where baselines fail.
- Weakness：
  - The current implementation only enforces gradient constraints at individual input points , not over neighborhoods or polytopes. While the paper mentions future extensions inspired by APRNN and PREPARED, this severely limits applicability in robustness and generalization settings. In practice, real-world safety constraints must hold across regions, not just isolated samples.
  - ProGrad’s "conditional variable gradient" (Def. 4.2) is an extension of APRNN’s conditional output. The chain rule (Eq. 16) directly applies APRNN’s framework to gradients, which seems to show little theoretical innovation beyond repurposing prior work.
  - The paper focuses on editing only the last few layers (typically the final layer) of the neural network. While this enables efficient and scalable editing of large models, it may limit the model’s ability to satisfy more complex or global gradient constraints that involve deeper layers.

questions.value: Does the method's restriction to editing only the final few layers affect its ability to enforce more complex or global gradient constraints? Could editing more layers improve constraint satisfaction, and what trade-offs might exist in terms of efficiency and performance?

limitations.value:
- ProGrad edits only the last few layers (often just the final layer) of the neural network. This may limit the model’s ability to satisfy more complex or global gradient constraints that involve deeper layers.
- As the author said, ProGrad currently enforces gradient constraints only on a finite set of input samples. It does not provide guarantees for broader input domains or structured input regions.

summary.value:
The paper introduces the problem of gradient editing wherein given a particular input to a network (here restricted to feed-forward networks with ReLU units), and a polyhedron within which the gradient  (or more accurately the Jacobian) of the network should lie, the approach computes changes to a subset of parameters, chosen so that the network is locally linear in these parameters. The approach builds upon similar ideas such as ARPNN that have appeared in the past (PLDI 2023), but extends to the problem of satisfying constraints
on the gradients rather than the outputs. The key idea is to formulate this as a linear program assuming that the change in the weights do not change the "activation patterns" of the various neurons in the network. The solution is applied to some very interesting case studies including enforcing "Grad-CAM" constraints on images wherein "Grad-CAM" refers to an approach to explainable classification wherein the gradient information is used to study some sort of sensitivity of the pixels to a classification. The paper uses the proposed gradient editing techniques to update weights of CNNs to make them robust to input perturbations. Other experimental evaluations include those on large language models and a place holder for a physical model with a gradient constraint.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
I enjoyed reading the paper for the most part. The writing and presentation were clear to me and the ideas were easy to see. I do have a few minor issues that I report at the end. 

+ The main strength of the paper lies in the applications. Although I am not an expert in the areas of computer vision or natural language processing, I found the applications to be well motivated and natural. I do not quite get the application to provably safe control systems: that application was illustrated by a rather artificial example that did not seem credible.

My key issues here are mostly about originality and some technical issues.

- Originality: I am not very sure about the  intellectual depth here. The idea that (i) fixing the activation patterns of the neuron linearizes a network is at the core of the paper and is hardly novel/original; (ii) the idea that one can modify a single layer's weights and the biases of the layers is also natural and has been explored by many authors even in the context of neural network repair. Nevertheless, a simple idea that can have practical impact is quite welcome.

- Technical applicability: I am not really sold that editing gradients at one input suffices. Clearly, it does not for most applications. However, the approach is limited to one layer at a time. I have been thinking about how one handles multiple inputs to the network whose gradients all need to lie within different polyhedra?  
   - It is not clear if editing a single layer at a time suffices. One imagines that multiple neurons across different layers may need to be modified. 
   - Editing more than one layer yields nonlinear (multilinear) constraints and approaches such as iterating between layers are well known not to be very good at solving these problems. 
   - Treating the inputs one by one is not going to work. Fixing for one input may invalidate a fix made for a previous input. 

Overall, interesting paper but I get the sense that the difficult problem has not been properly addressed here. Rather, a  simpler version is presented and it is unclear that ideas extend readily.

title.value: Provable Gradient Editing of Deep Neural Networks

TLDR.value: Efficient technique for enforcing hard constraints on the gradients of DNN by editing the DNN parameters.

abstract.value: In explainable AI, DNN gradients are used to interpret the prediction; in safety-critical control systems, gradients could encode safety constraints; in scientific-computing applications, gradients could encode physical invariants. While recent work on provable editing of DNNs has focused on input-output constraints, the problem of enforcing hard constraints on DNN gradients remains unaddressed. We present ProGrad, the first efficient approach for editing the parameters of a DNN to provably enforce hard constraints on the DNN gradients. Given a DNN $\mathcal{N}$ with parameters $\theta$, and a set $\mathcal{S}$ of pairs $(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{Q})$ of input $\mathrm{x}$ and corresponding linear gradient constraints $\mathrm{Q}$, ProGrad finds new parameters $\theta'$ such that $\bigwedge_{(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{Q}) \in \mathcal{S}} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathrm{x}}\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{x}; \theta') \in \mathrm{Q}$ while minimizing the changes $\lVert\theta' - \theta\rVert$. The key contribution is a novel *conditional variable gradient* of DNNs, which relaxes the NP-hard provable gradient editing problem to a linear program (LP), enabling ProGrad to use an LP solver to efficiently and effectively enforce the gradient constraints. We experimentally evaluated ProGrad via enforcing (i) hard Grad-CAM constraints on ImageNet ResNet DNNs; (ii) hard Integrated Gradients constraints on Llama 3 and Qwen 3 LLMs; (iii) hard gradient constraints in training a DNN to approximate a target function as a proxy for safety constraints in control systems and physical invariants in scientific applications. The results highlight the unique capability of ProGrad in enforcing hard constraints on DNN gradients.
